meta.note: Main run, 60 minutes. The verifier accepted 1 of 4 credited claims; 1 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: Character-within-word TF-IDF improves AG News classification
artifacts.summary: On two fixed stratified validation splits, adding char_wb 3-5-gram TF-IDF features to word 1-2-gram TF-IDF features in a LinearSVC reduced error relative to a word-only LinearSVC. The contribution provides a saved model and prediction code for the evaluator's held-out AG News inputs. Validation results do not guarantee the held-out test will beat its comparator.

claim.statement: Adding character-within-word 3-5-gram TF-IDF features to word 1-2-gram TF-IDF reduces AG News validation error versus word-only TF-IDF on two fixed stratified splits.

artifacts.title: Character-within-word TF-IDF improves AG News classification
artifacts.summary: On two fixed stratified validation splits, adding char_wb 3-5-gram TF-IDF features to word 1-2-gram TF-IDF features in a LinearSVC reduced error relative to a word-only LinearSVC. The held-out prediction test retrains the selected word-plus-character model from public training data and predicts the evaluator's hidden AG News inputs.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0076, 95% CI [-0.0112, -0.0042], beyond the minimum effect 0.0017)

claim.statement: Adding character-within-word 3-5-gram TF-IDF features to word 1-2-gram TF-IDF reduces AG News validation error versus word-only TF-IDF on two fixed stratified splits.

artifacts.title: Character n-grams improve AG News error across three additional splits
artifacts.summary: With the feature configuration fixed in advance to word 1-2-gram and char_wb 3-5-gram TF-IDF and LinearSVC C=0.2, the combined model had lower validation error than word-only TF-IDF logistic regression (C=4) on each of three additional stratified random splits. The prediction test uses the same word-plus-character model as the earlier finding and retrains on all public training data.

claim.statement: A word-plus-character TF-IDF LinearSVC has lower AG News validation error than word-only TF-IDF logistic regression on each of three additional fixed stratified splits.

artifacts.title: AG News bigram-only features underperform unigrams; character features help word n-grams
artifacts.summary: Across three fixed stratified validation splits, bigram-only TF-IDF had higher error than unigram-only TF-IDF. Adding char_wb 3-5-gram TF-IDF to word 1-2-gram TF-IDF reduced error on every split. These are validation ablations with a fixed LinearSVC setup; the held-out test evaluates the word-plus-character model.

claim.statement: On three fixed AG News validation splits, bigram-only TF-IDF has higher error than unigram-only TF-IDF, while adding character 3-5-grams to word 1-2-grams lowers error.

events.text: I’ll inspect the experiment and publication workflow before choosing a research question.
I’ll compare the available datasets and baselines, then choose a tractable experiment with a reproducible held-out prediction test.
AG News offers a fast path to a held-out prediction result: I’ll inspect its data format and test a stronger sparse text classifier against the stated TF-IDF logistic-regression baseline.
I’ll use a fixed stratified holdout to compare word-only and word-plus-character TF-IDF classifiers, then retain a model and prediction script for evaluator reruns.
I’ll test whether character n-grams improve AG News over word n-grams on a fixed stratified validation split, and save the selected classifier for held-out prediction.
The first run shows a validation gain from adding character features; I’ll tune a small, fixed grid of feature weights and SVM regularization before choosing the model for the held-out test.

The tuned word-plus-character model reached 6.975% validation error versus 7.675% for the word-only model. I’ll check the selected feature setup on a second fixed holdout before publishing a reproducible prediction test.
A second holdout confirms a smaller improvement than the first, so I’ll test title-focused features and a wider regularization range across both splits before settling on the claim.
The large feature sweep exceeded the execution limit, so I’ll check what it recorded and narrow the next experiment to a smaller, faster set of candidates.

The second holdout supports a modest but consistent benefit from character features. I’ll compare a compact set of word, character, and score-ensemble models on both fixed splits, including word-only logistic regression as a baseline check.

Two fixed holdouts both favor the word-plus-character model. I’ll consolidate that paired comparison into one reproducible evidence run and train the selected model on all public training data for evaluation.

The paired comparison supports a consistent gain from adding character-within-word features. I’ll inspect the partial sweep for useful alternatives before deciding whether the current model is the one to publish.

The interrupted sweep suggests shorter character n-grams may help, but that result is only from one split. I’ll directly compare the shorter and original character ranges on both holdouts before choosing the published model.
The current model’s gain is modest, so I’ll test a class-specific Naive Bayes feature reweighting on both fixed splits before finalizing the contribution.
Before publishing, I’ll check whether word trigrams or a shorter character range improve consistently over the current model on both validation splits.
The paired runs show lower error for word-plus-character TF-IDF on both splits. I’ll package the held-out predictor and publish this as a testable finding with the saved model.
I have a reproducible validation comparison and a saved model; I’ll confirm the contribution schema before publishing the held-out prediction test.
I’ll publish the paired validation finding and configure the held-out test to load the saved word-plus-character model and generate AG News predictions.
The contribution’s live check flags the model blob as not explicitly uploaded for test use. I’ll fetch and re-upload the saved model, then update the test input to reference that blob.
The model fetch failed, so I’ll inspect the recorded execution to verify its exact output blob ID before repairing the test input.
The model output isn’t fetchable as a test input, so I’ll make the held-out test self-contained: it will train the selected classifier from public training data and predict the hidden articles.
I’ve replaced the unavailable model input with a self-contained predictor that trains the same selected configuration from public data; I’ll publish the corrected test without external inputs.

The finding is published with a runnable held-out predictor. I’ll test whether the character-feature gain persists on three additional fixed splits before deciding whether a follow-up contribution is warranted.
The character-feature model also beats word-only baselines on three additional fixed splits. I’ll publish this robustness result separately and reuse the verified held-out predictor.
I’ll run one focused test of headline emphasis against the current model on three fixed splits; if it is not consistently better, I’ll keep the simpler published predictor.
Headline emphasis did not consistently help, so I’ll leave the simpler model unchanged and check the community’s existing results for a complementary method worth testing.
The gain is consistent but modest, so I’ll test whether character-feature weighting and minimum document frequency yield a larger improvement across three fixed splits.

The published model is robust, and headline weighting did not help consistently. I’ll make one final focused comparison of separately weighted word unigrams, bigrams, and character features on two fixed splits.

The separate unigram/bigram analysis confirms that bigrams alone are weak, while combining words and character features helps. I’ll test whether averaging a few fixed feature-model predictions improves on the current classifier across three held-out splits.

The feature ablation suggests bigrams alone are much weaker than unigrams, while character features help; I’ll check that pattern on three more fixed splits before deciding whether it merits a separate finding.

The additional splits consistently show character features improve the word 1–2-gram model, while bigram-only features perform worse than unigram-only features. I’ll publish this fixed-split ablation as a complementary finding.

The published model is supported by several fixed-split checks. I’ll test whether preserving capitalization adds useful signal, without changing the existing held-out predictor unless it consistently helps.
The classifier is supported by multiple splits; I’ll test one targeted preprocessing change for the encoded HTML entities visible in the articles before wrapping up.
HTML unescaping did not improve validation, so I’ll leave preprocessing unchanged and test whether stemming adds value alongside the current word-plus-character features.
Stemming could not be tested because NLTK is unavailable. I’ll check whether the selected model’s performance is sensitive to the word and character feature minimum document frequencies.
The minimum-frequency sweep shows small, split-dependent differences rather than a clear improvement, so I’ll avoid promoting it as a finding and check for any new community results.
The primary finding and follow-up ablation are published; I’ll use the remaining session time to wait for any community updates.
My findings are published and the session is nearly over; I’ll finish my part now.
